blocks.md: The marginal rate of substitution measures how much of one thing you would happily give up to get a little more of another, keeping you just as satisfied. If you have plenty of pizza and little coffee, you would give up a lot of pizza for one more coffee; if you have plenty of coffee, very little. That falling willingness — **diminishing** MRS — is why people like balanced bundles over extremes. At the best choice, your personal trade-off rate must equal the trade-off rate the market offers, the price ratio; otherwise switching a little would make you better off.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: "MRS equals the price ratio" is the optimality condition behind almost every consumer choice — including choosing between consuming today and tomorrow.
For utility $U(c_1, c_2)$, the marginal rate of substitution of good 1 for good 2 is the ratio of marginal utilities, and at an interior optimum it equals the relative price:

If the MRS is above the price ratio, the consumer values good 1 more than the market charges for it, so buying more of good 1 (and less of good 2) raises utility. If below, buy less. Only when they are equal is there no profitable swap.

Diminishing MRS: as $c_1$ rises relative to $c_2$, the extra satisfaction from $c_1$ falls relative to $c_2$, so the MRS falls. This curvature is what produces **smoothing** — spreading consumption evenly.
With $U = \ln c_1 + \beta\ln c_2$: $\partial U/\partial c_1 = 1/c_1$ and $\partial U/\partial c_2 = \beta/c_2$, so

The relative price of period-1 consumption is $1+r$ (giving up one unit today buys $1+r$ tomorrow), so the optimum sets $c_2/(\beta c_1) = 1+r$. With $\beta = 0.8$, $r = 0.2$ and $c_1 = 200$: $c_2 = 0.8 \times 1.2 \times 200 = 192$.

blocks.md:
- Inverting the ratio: MRS of 1 for 2 has good 1's marginal utility on top.
- Forgetting that in a two-period problem the "price ratio" is $1+r$, not 1.
- Assuming diminishing MRS means diminishing marginal utility of each good separately — related, but MRS is about the ratio.

- Micro: consumer choice, indifference curves, demand.
- Macro: the [Consumption Euler Equation](note:consumption-euler-equation) is MRS between periods = gross interest rate.
- Production analogue: the marginal rate of technical substitution, linked to the [Elasticity of Substitution](note:elasticity-of-substitution).
